The guy whose AI photo app does $105,000 a month with zero employees, on Lex Fridman: "I don't raise money. I do everything myself. I'm the designer, I'm the developer, I make the logo."

This is him explaining how one person ships that fast - and the thing that slows everybody else down.

He builds an idea in two weeks, launches it, and drops it if nobody pays.

Then he points at Google. It had the data, the tech and the engineers to ship ChatGPT first, and shipped nothing.

He works from a laptop in shorts, on vanilla PHP, jQuery and SQLite.

Founder friends sitting on hundreds of millions in funding tell him privately they would do it his way next time.

Every number he posts is public, and every one of them was built by one person.

Watch him defend working alone, then start the ladder in the article below.

Hundreds of billions of dollars are lent overnight on security and then repaid the following morning in 2008 that system came to an end, and almost no one attends the lecture which explains it.

Gary Gorton from Yale, standing on the lectern at a law school, is going over what actually broke.

There was no waiting outside the branches; the withdrawals took place between institutions and were charged in the form of haircuts on securities which no one could value.

Look at the part in which he demonstrates how a small change to that haircut eliminates the borrower.

The run could not be seen since the depositors were banks.

Anthropic is on a $47 billion run rate and still burning most of it on compute. Every token you send them is a cost they pass straight to you.

You're not buying intelligence. You're renting it, per query, forever.

And RAG rents the dumb way. Twenty chunks pulled, nineteen unrelated, the full bill on all twenty.

Worse, it re-buys the same reasoning every single time you ask.

A graph pays once. Extract the entities and edges up front, then never re-derive them again.

The token spend was never the real loss. The real loss is owning nothing when it's over.

Burn $10,000 in API calls on retrieval and you have receipts. Spend it building a graph and you have an asset.

One depreciates the second the next model ships. The other gets denser every document you add.

That's the split nobody prices: rented answers versus a structure you keep.

The labs need the first. Their whole valuation assumes you never choose the second.

Don't let this die in your bookmarks. Save it, add up last month's retrieval spend, and put the same money into a graph you'll still own next year.

OpenAI raised at $852 billion. Anthropic just cleared $965 billion. Both business models quietly need your data to stay trapped inside their API.

That's the trade you signed. Your knowledge lives as loose text, and you rent intelligence by the token to make sense of it.

Every query ships the whole pile back to them. You pay frontier rate to re-read what you already own.

RAG made that feel efficient. It isn't. Twenty chunks retrieved, nineteen noise, all twenty billed.

And it still can't answer what sits across three documents that share no words.

A graph moves the intelligence to your side. Extract the structure once, then walk paths you own.

The connection isn't rented anymore. It's stored, and every query after is nearly free.

Here's what breaks the rent: Kimi K3's weights are public. The extractor now runs on your hardware, not their meter.

So the one expensive step - turning documents into a graph - stops paying a lab at all.

Two labs are worth nearly two trillion combined betting you never move that step in-house.

Don't let this rot in your bookmarks.

Save it, point K3 at your documents tonight, and build the graph the meter was counting on you to keep renting.
